metadata.title: Banking Domain Data Analyst Interview Prep — the SQL Banks Actually Ask
metadata.description: The whole-book trailer: banking DA interviews add a regulatory/ratio/fraud-instinct layer on top of general SQL and Python. Two real worked examples carry the build-with-Claude loop — Ch.8's correct running-balance CTE (sum-before-filter) and Ch.9's cohort-preserving vintage-curve query (Harborline Card Co.) — bookended by the book's six-part map.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — open on the Claude UI, ask shown answered
beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Supriya and this video is about the SQL that banking interviews actually ask. You already know SQL. That's not what trips people up.

props.command: claude "what's the banking-specific gap in my data-analyst interview prep?"

beats.role_note: why care — stated before the CLI loop begins; SHOW-DON'T-TELL LAW: Manim, not a static card
beats.narration_text: A general analytics interview tests joins, cohorts, and dashboards: skills you already have. A banking one adds a second language on top: regulators like the OCC and the CFPB, ratios like CET1 and LCR, and the habit of asking whether a number is regulatory-reportable, or could be fraud.
beats.visual_intent: SQL and Python tiles slide in and lock together (a skillset already solid); a second, translucent layer of terms — CET1 · LCR · OCC · CFPB · charge-off — slides in on top and snaps opaque, labeled 'the layer banking adds'

beats.role_note: the book's own map — six parts
beats.narration_text: This book maps that layer in six parts: the banking landscape, regulation and risk, the modern data stack, technical prep with forty-plus SQL problems and Python for banking, the behavioral and case rounds, and a day-of cheat sheet.
beats.visual_intent: six labeled blocks build left-to-right into a single pipeline (Landscape → Regulation/Risk → Data Stack → Technical Prep → Behavioral/Case/Systems → Day-Of), each locking in with a soft snap as its name is spoken

beats.narration_text: Take one worked problem from chapter eight: end-of-month balances for the first half of twenty twenty-six, built one CTE at a time.

props.command: claude "review this running-balance query: end-of-month balances for Jan–Jun 2026, one CTE at a time"

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — cycle 1, the correct query (Ch.8, no bug reconstruction)
beats.narration_text: Here's the shape. Running computes the cumulative balance over the whole ledger, with no WHERE clause at all. One CTE later, the date filter narrows to the reporting window and keeps each month's last posting. Sum first. Filter after.

props.title: running_balance_fixed.mysql.sql (excerpt)
props.code:
WITH running AS (
  SELECT account_id, transaction_id, posted_at,
    SUM(amount) OVER (
      PARTITION BY account_id
      ORDER BY posted_at, transaction_id
      ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
    ) AS running_balance
  -- no WHERE: the whole ledger
  FROM transactions
),
last_posting_per_month AS (
  -- … ROW_NUMBER() … AS rn
  FROM running
  -- moved here: after the sum
  WHERE posted_at >= '2026-01-01'
    AND posted_at <  '2026-07-01'
),

beats.narration_text: Run it on a Cascade Savings account that carried twelve thousand four hundred dollars into January. The month-end balances on screen are the true ones, because the sum saw the whole ledger first.
beats.visual_intent: 3-row EOM table builds top-to-bottom (Jan/Feb/Mar), each value landing in teal: 12,100.00 / 12,250.00 / 12,175.00; small annotation ties Jan's value back to the Nov 2025 deposit crossing the year boundary

beats.role_note: composer (ClaudeComposerAsk) — cycle 2, the required revision. SPARK-LINE LAW: CHANGE beat carries the ask itself as its spark, no separate greeting.
beats.narration_text: That's one shape. Chapter nine adds a harder one, on a different dataset: a card issuer's monthly snapshots, where the job is to keep one cohort intact.

props.command: claude "chapter nine: build the Jan 2025 cohort's delinquency mix at 3, 6 and 9 months on book"

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — cycle 2, the cohort-preserving query (Ch.9, Harborline Card Co.)
beats.narration_text: Isolate the January twenty twenty-five cohort first. Compute months on book by diffing each snapshot against the origination month. Then group by months on book and bucket. A calendar-month group-by would lose the cohort.

props.title: vintage_curve.mysql.sql (excerpt)
props.code:
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT account_id
  FROM   accounts
  WHERE  origination_month = '2025-01-01'
),
snap AS (
  SELECT s.account_id, s.dpd_bucket,
    PERIOD_DIFF(
      DATE_FORMAT(s.snapshot_month, '%Y%m'),
      DATE_FORMAT(a.origination_month, '%Y%m')
    ) AS months_on_book
),
bucketed AS (
  SELECT months_on_book, dpd_bucket,
    COUNT(*) AS accounts_in_bucket,
    -- , SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (…) AS cohort_total
  GROUP BY months_on_book, dpd_bucket
)

beats.narration_text: Run it on a Harborline sample cohort. At month three, ninety-two percent are current. By month nine, four percent are ninety-plus days past due and three percent charged off. Each column adds back to five hundred, because this sample has one snapshot per account per month.
beats.visual_intent: a 3-column (3/6/9 months) stacked-bar build, each column's segments landing bucket by bucket (current→30→60→90+→charge_off), a running 'of 500' cohort-total label pinned above every column so it visibly never changes

beats.narration_text: Two moves: get the SQL evaluation order right, and never lose the cohort. That's chapters eight and nine. The rest of the book covers regulatory metrics, the data stack, and the behavioral and case rounds.
beats.visual_intent: 2-line checklist builds with checkmarks ('get the SQL order right' / 'never lose the cohort'), then the six-part map from B02 re-appears compressed beneath it as a 'the rest of the book' tag

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — the suggested prompt read aloud and discussed, not just shown
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Try this: Check my banking SQL for two bugs: is any date filter applied before a running SUM() OVER, and does every row stay tied to its cohort? Both bugs run without an error, so the only way to find them is to ask.
